clinicalPearls: A genetically heterogeneous group defined by pure, length-dependent distal motor weakness and wasting without significant sensory loss, distinguishing it from Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease
Because it affects motor axons or anterior horn cells selectively, it is also termed distal spinal muscular atrophy or spinal CMT
Weakness usually begins in the feet and lower legs with foot drop and pes cavus, later involving the hands in many subtypes
Numerous causative genes are recognised (for example HSPB1, HSPB8, GARS1, BSCL2, DYNC1H1), inherited in dominant, recessive or X-linked patterns

Some subtypes have distinctive features such as predominant hand and upper-limb onset, vocal cord or diaphragmatic involvement, or pyramidal signs overlapping with hereditary spastic paraplegia and motor neuron disease
Nerve conduction studies show reduced motor amplitudes with preserved sensory responses, and EMG confirms chronic denervation
Sensory nerve action potentials being normal is the key electrophysiological discriminator from CMT
Management is supportive, with physiotherapy, orthoses (e.g. ankle-foot orthoses), footwear and occupational therapy
reference.pathophysiology: The distal hereditary motor neuropathies are inherited disorders in which the pathology is largely restricted to the motor system, involving distal motor axons and/or anterior horn cells with relative sparing of sensory neurons. The many causative genes converge on core neuronal processes essential for long motor axons, including axonal transport (for example dynein and kinesin components), protein folding and chaperone function (small heat-shock proteins such as HSPB1 and HSPB8), aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase activity (GARS1) and lipid metabolism (BSCL2). Disruption of these pathways causes a length-dependent, dying-back degeneration of the longest motor fibres, producing progressive distal weakness and wasting.
additionalDifferentials: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (which additionally involves sensory fibres)
Spinal muscular atrophy and other motor neuron disorders
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and other motor neuron disease when upper motor neuron signs coexist
Chronic inflammatory or multifocal motor neuropathy (treatable acquired mimics)
Distal myopathies presenting with distal weakness
Hereditary spastic paraplegia in subtypes with pyramidal features
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies showing reduced motor amplitudes with normal sensory responses
Electromyography demonstrating chronic distal denervation and reinnervation
Targeted or panel genetic testing across the many dHMN-associated genes
MRI of muscle to characterise the pattern of involvement in selected cases
Exclusion of treatable acquired motor neuropathies (e.g. multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block)
Respiratory and, where relevant, laryngoscopic assessment in subtypes with diaphragmatic or vocal cord involvement
redFlags: Prominent or progressing upper motor neuron signs and bulbar involvement suggesting motor neuron disease
Diaphragmatic weakness causing respiratory compromise in specific subtypes
Vocal cord paralysis with stridor or airway risk
Rapid progression or conduction block pointing to a treatable acquired neuropathy
reference.prognosis: Most distal hereditary motor neuropathies progress slowly, remain confined to the distal limbs and do not shorten life; disability arises mainly from foot drop, hand weakness and deformity, though rare subtypes with respiratory or bulbar involvement carry a more serious outlook.
pitfalls: Labelling the condition Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease without noting the preserved sensory responses that define dHMN
Missing a treatable acquired motor neuropathy such as multifocal motor neuropathy
Overlooking respiratory or vocal cord involvement in subtypes where it occurs
Failing to recognise overlap with motor neuron disease when pyramidal signs are present
